papers.title: Repeated exposure to a conserved antigen drives dynamic clonal and epitope succession
papers.authors: Aoki, H.; Pogorelyy, M. V.; Bradley, P.; Adragna, C.; Schattgen, S. A.; Minervina, A. A.; Mayer-Blackwell, K. H.; Vegesana, K.; Scott, Z. B.; Balaraman, V.; Allen, E. K.; Kitabatake, M.; Ouji-Sageshima, N.; Hara, A.; Xu, P.; Motozono, C.; Matsushima, K.; Sallusto, F.; Lanzavecchia, A.; Ueha, S.; Ito, T.; Thomas, P. G.
papers.abstract: Defining the dynamics of T cell memory formation with epitope-level resolution can inform vaccine design. Longitudinal T cell receptor (TCR) sequencing after COVID-19 mRNA vaccination has enabled detailed tracking of T cell responses; however, connecting expanded clonotypes following antigen exposure to their cognate epitopes remains a challenge due to limited curated paired /{beta}TCR information. To fill this gap, we used TIRTL-seq to identify paired /{beta}TCRs from CD8+ T cell lineages associated with mRNA immunization in serial samples across 38 healthy donors over multiple rounds of vaccinations. Vaccine-associated paired /{beta}TCRs, identified based on their longitudinal kinetics, were grouped according to sequence similarity to infer their shared epitope specificities. We assigned epitope specificity to 1,109 clonotypes, recognizing 15 SARS-CoV-2 spike targets, identifying multiple previously undescribed responses, and confirming putative specificities experimentally. This approach uncovered a striking pattern of clonal succession in anti-spike T cell memory lineages resulting from repeated vaccination, characterized by a transition from low-avidity clones recognizing conserved coronavirus epitopes to high-avidity clones targeting epitopes unique to SARS-CoV-2. These results highlight the surprisingly dynamic responses underlying homologous boosting, suggest avenues for improving vaccine strategies, and pave the way for repertoire-based monitoring of antigen-specific T cell immunity.

papers.title: Single-cell Profiling of Airway-associated CD4+ T cells in Metal-induced Hypersensitivity
papers.authors: Ypil, J.; Fu, R. M.; Raza, M.; Li, L.; Maier, L.; Fontenot, A. P.; Dinarello, C. A.; Atif, S. M.
papers.abstract: Omics-based approaches are increasingly used to identify unique molecular signatures that may serve as biomarkers for early disease detection and potential therapeutic targets. Chronic beryllium disease (CBD), resulting from beryllium-induced hypersensitivity, is characterized by the accumulation and expansion of pathogenic CD4+ T cells in the lungs, ultimately contributing to impaired pulmonary function. In this study, we performed single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) on sorted viable bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) cells from beryllium-exposed patients (n=2) and compared their transcriptional profiles with publicly available scRNA-seq datasets from healthy controls (n=10). We identified 11 distinct CD3-associated cell clusters comprising T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, and regulatory T cells. Further analysis of CD4+ T cells from beryllium-exposed patients revealed increased expression of genes associated with T cell activation, immune regulation, and persistence, including IFNG, TNF, TNFAIP3, and CD74. Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis further revealed upregulation of pathways associated with cellular activation, immune responses, and immune effector functions, whereas pathways related to metabolic processes were downregulated in beryllium samples compared with healthy controls. Overall, our findings identify distinct transcriptional signatures, including IFI27 and FABP4, in CD4+ T cells from beryllium-exposed patients, providing insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying beryllium-induced pulmonary inflammation and highlighting potential candidates for further investigation as disease biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

papers.title: Reinvigorating immunotherapy: harnessing tumor microenvironment modulation for enhanced cancer treatment.
papers.authors: Wu B, Zhang W, Shu Y, Chen X, Yang K, Hu J.
papers.abstract: Cancer immunotherapy has transformed the treatment of multiple malignancies, yet primary and acquired resistance remain major barriers to attaining durable clinical benefit. Increasing evidence indicates that immunotherapy failure rarely results from a single mechanism but instead emerges from dynamic interactions within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Recent advances in single-cell, spatial multiomics, and longitudinal profiling have revealed the complex organization of TME-mediated resistance, which can be conceptualized within three interconnected suppressive modules: the tumor-cell-intrinsic module, myeloid-suppressive networks, and stromal barriers. The relative dominance of these modules varies across spatial niches, metastatic sites, disease stages, and treatment phases, leading to profound spatiotemporal heterogeneity and dynamic reorganization of dominant resistance axes. In this Review, we propose a spatiotemporal and systems-level framework for understanding TME-mediated immunotherapy resistance. We discuss how the tumor-cell-intrinsic module contributes to immune escape, how myeloid-suppressive networks and stromal barriers sustain and amplify immunosuppression, and how reciprocal crosstalk among these modules generates feed-forward loops that stabilize resistant states. We also review clinical strategies for remodeling the TME to increase the efficacy of immunotherapeutic approaches. Additionally, we discuss the opportunities and challenges associated with TME remodeling, including safety considerations, emerging biomarkers, and rational combination strategies. We propose that future TME-targeted therapies should transition from component-oriented interventions to dynamic and mechanism-matched strategies guided by dominant resistance axes. This approach aims to facilitate the development of more precise and durable cancer immunotherapies.

papers.title: Microglial Metabolic Reprogramming Regulated by HIF-1α/HK2 Positive Feedback Inhibits Adult Hippocampal Neurogenesis in Diabetes-Associated Cognitive Dysfunction.
papers.authors: Jiang S, Zhao Y, Zhang Q, Zhang J, Gao Z, Luo Y, Zhao N, Guo N, An C, Zhang R, Liu Z, Xu S.
papers.abstract: Diabetes-associated cognitive dysfunction (DACD) is a significant complication with few effective treatments and unclear underlying mechanism. The aim of this study was to investigate how hyperglycemia disrupts adult hippocampal neurogenesis (AHN) through metabolic-immune interactions, seeking to identify potential treatment targets for DACD. DACD models were developed using db/db mice or streptozotocin-induced mice, and their cognitive function was assessed through behavioral tests. Next, we integrated multi-omics analyses (transcriptomic, single-cell, and lactylome profiling) with metabolic studies in BV2 cells exposed to diabetic conditions. Pharmacological modulators (3-BP, C646, TSA) were used to clarify the underlying mechanisms. The mice with DACD demonstrated cognitive deficits, impaired AHN, and activation of hippocampal microglia. Transcriptomic analysis revealed glycolysis as the primary dysregulated pathway. Mechanistically, hyperglycemia/AGEs induced glycolytic reprogramming and increased lactate levels, which promoted HIF-1α lactylation at lysine residues-a modification catalyzed by p300 and opposed by histone deacetylases. This posttranslational modification was associated with HIF-1α stabilisation and with enhanced transcriptional occupancy at the HK2 promoter. This established a self-amplifying feedback loop, perpetuating microglial activation and disrupting the blood-brain barrier via CXCL10 secretion, which led to CD8 + T-cell infiltration. Systemic administration of the glycolytic inhibitor 3-BP disrupted the pathogenic circuit, thereby normalizing metabolism, attenuating neuroinflammation, and restoring cognitive function. HIF-1α lactylation is associated with HIF-1α stabilisation, acting as a potential metabolic-epigenetic mechanism that links glycolytic flux to sustained microglial activation, neuroinflammation and impaired AHN in DACD. Pharmacological inhibition of this axis attenuated neuroinflammation and improved cognitive outcomes in our model, suggesting a candidate therapeutic strategy for DACD.

papers.title: RIPK2 influences bone metastasis in prostate cancer through macrophage-tumor cell interaction: a mechanistic study.
papers.authors: Zhao H, Wu D, Ren R, Ni L.
papers.abstract: Background Bone metastasis is a leading cause of mortality in prostate cancer (PCa) patients with limited treatment options. Myeloid-tumor cell interactions in the tumor microenvironment (TME) critically drive metastasis, but the mechanisms involved are poorly understood. Elucidating the myeloid-tumor cell crosstalk is crucial for developing novel anti-metastatic therapies. Methods Myeloid and tumor cell subsets were identified through single-cell RNA sequencing and copy number variation (CNV) analysis. Key signaling axes between these subsets were identified through cell-cell communication analysis. Molecular biological experiments, including qRT-PCR, Western blot, and flow cytometry, were conducted to investigate the effects of RIPK2 + macrophages on malignant tumor cell phenotypes. Results RIPK2 + macrophages and disseminated tumor cells (DTCs) were enriched in tumor samples. DTCs exhibited high CNV scores and metastatic potential. RIPK2 + macrophages displayed unique antigen-presenting and immunoregulatory characteristics and engaged in high-intensity interactions with DTCs via the THBS1-CD47 signaling axis. In vitro, RIPK2 upregulated THBS1 and CD47, promoted their protein interaction, and enhanced PCa cell proliferation, migration, and invasion while repressing apoptosis. Conclusions Revealed by single-cell sequencing and molecular biological experiments, RIPK2 + macrophages promote PCa bone metastasis through the THBS1-CD47 axis. The findings expand the understanding of myeloid-tumor cell interaction networks in the TME and provide a theoretical basis for developing TME-targeted therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Deciphering the molecular mechanisms linking abnormal mitochondrial respiratory chain activity to myeloid cell activation in systemic lupus erythematosus through multi-scale transcriptomics.
papers.authors: Qiu J, Fang T, Yao X, Ye K, Wang X.
papers.abstract: Abnormal mitochondrial respiratory chain (MRC) activity is a pivotal driver in the pathogenesis of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). However, the molecular mechanisms linking it to immune phenotypes and disease progression remain unclear. This study aims to systematically determine core biomarkers of MRC dysfunction in SLE and explore their potential pathogenic mechanisms through multi-scale transcriptomic analysis. Five bulk transcriptomic series from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) were integrated to screen for differentially expressed genes linked to MRC abnormalities. Three machine learning algorithms and SHAP analysis were applied to identify core signature genes. Leveraging these markers, a diagnostic model was developed, along with constructing molecular interaction and regulatory networks. We elucidated the biological functions through functional enrichment, immune infiltration analyzes, and correlation analysis with key therapeutic targets. Furthermore, we integrated three single-cell datasets and applied Seurat clustering, pseudotime analysis, and CellChat to characterize the expression patterns, differentiation trajectories, and interaction networks of core genes within specific cell subpopulations. Our results identified 18 biomarkers, with SCO2 emerging as the primary core gene. The diagnostic model achieved high discriminatory accuracy. Multi-dimensional functional analyzes uncovered a potential role for SCO2 bridging mitochondrial metabolic dysfunction with antiviral innate immune activation. Single-cell analysis localized SCO2 overexpression primarily to monocytes and dendritic cells, showing a downregulation trajectory during myeloid differentiation. We found that SCO2 + myeloid cells exhibit altered interaction networks within the immune microenvironment, characterized by enriched MHC-I/II and MIF signaling. In conclusion, SCO2 is a critical biomarker of MRC activity in SLE, reflecting the mitochondrial metabolic reprogramming that drives immune dysregulation.

papers.title: A Synthetic Benchmark for Topology-Aware Modeling of Multispecific Antibody Function.
papers.authors: Southern J, Lu C, Nerli S, Stanton SD, Watkins AM, Seeger F, Dreyer FA.
papers.abstract: Multispecific antibodies (msAbs) offer transformative therapeutic potential by engaging multiple epitopes simultaneously, yet their efficacy is an emergent property governed by complex molecular architectures. Rational design is often bottlenecked by the inability to predict how subtle changes in domain topology influence functional outcomes, a challenge exacerbated by the scarcity of comprehensive experimental data. Here, we introduce Synapse, a biologically inspired synthetic benchmark for topology-aware modeling of msAbs. First, we present a generative method that combines nonlinear per-domain sequence-to-score landscapes with connectivity-dependent synthetic readouts. Second, we propose a graph neural network architecture that explicitly encodes these topological constraints, distinguishing between format configurations that appear identical to the evaluated connectivity-agnostic multilayer perceptron. We demonstrate that this model learns topology-dependent structure-function relationships on synthetic landscapes and evaluate a transfer learning workflow as infrastructure for adaptation to biological datasets. We showcase our framework with a trispecific T cell engager-inspired synthetic topology-dependent optimization task and a constrained ranking of common light chain candidates against a composite objective. This work provides a controlled benchmarking environment for developing and evaluating topology-aware computational tools for msAb modeling. All experiments use synthetic data; no biological validation is performed.

papers.title: Lemonite: identification of regulatory metabolites through data-driven, interpretable integration of transcriptomics and metabolomics data
papers.authors: Vandemoortele, B.; Devlies, H.; Michoel, T.; Vanhaecke, L.; Vandenbroucke, R. E.; Laukens, D.; Vermeirssen, V.
papers.abstract: Biological regulation emerges from coordinated interactions between genes, proteins, and metabolites; yet, despite their central regulatory potential, metabolites remain largely absent from genome-wide gene regulatory network inference. Current transcriptomics-metabolomics integration approaches are either limited by poor interpretability or constrained by incomplete prior knowledge, preventing the systematic identification of regulatory metabolites. Here, we present Lemonite, a data-driven and interpretable framework for integrating bulk transcriptomics and metabolomics data to uncover regulatory metabolites acting on gene modules. Lemonite extends module network inference to jointly associate transcription factors and metabolites with coexpressed gene programs, without requiring prior differential analysis or complete metabolite annotation. To contextualize predictions, we construct a comprehensive gene-metabolite knowledge graph integrating over 370,000 metabolite-gene and 2.1 million protein-protein interactions. Applied to glioblastoma and inflammatory bowel disease cohorts, Lemonite identifies over 50 functionally coherent gene modules per disease, revealing established and previously uncharacterized metabolite-gene regulatory relationships. In glioblastoma, myo-inositol and phosphatidylcholines, together with IRF6, regulate mesenchymal-like immune programs, which upon integration with single-cell transcriptomics are primarily expressed in tumor-associated macrophages and monocytes. In inflammatory bowel disease, regulatory metabolites are prioritized that change the expression of their predicted target genes in vitro. Together, Lemonite provides a principled framework to explore the genome-wide regulatory potential of the metabolome and to generate biologically interpretable, experimentally testable hypotheses from multi-omics data.

papers.title: Ciliated keratinocytes define a spatially restricted pro-inflammatory state in psoriasis and atopic dermatitis
papers.authors: Ike, M.; Hayashi, Y.; Nakamura, M.; He, H.; Nakaoku, A.; Ishii, K. J.; Fujita, F.; Motooka, D.; Toriyama, M.; Morita, A.
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Psoriasis vulgaris (Pso) and atopic dermatitis (AD) are characterized by recurrent flares and incomplete disease resolution. Primary cilia are antenna-like sensory organelles that project from the cell surface and coordinate extracellular signaling. Although epidermal ciliated cells are rarely detected in healthy skin and are selectively increased in AD and Pso, their molecular identity, functional properties, and clinical relevance remain unclear. Objective: To characterize epidermal ciliated cells in Pso and AD and determine their molecular identity, functional properties, and clinical relevance. Methods: We integrated single-cell-resolved spatial transcriptomics with primary cilia immunostaining in healthy skin (n=6), AD lesions (n=10), and paired psoriatic skin before and after phototherapy (n=7 each). Functional analyses using HaCaT cells with increased primary cilia formation included MAPK/NFkB signaling assays, ATAC-seq, and pathway inhibition assays. Results: Ciliated cells were largely restricted to AD and both pre and post treatment psoriatic skin, with KCs accounting for more than 70% of all ciliated cells. Ciliated KCs were predominantly localized to the basal and spinous layers. These cells exhibited disease and stage specific inflammatory programs and formed spatially organized communication networks with surrounding cells, including non ciliated KCs, fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and myeloid cells, suggesting a ciliated KC centered inflammation niche. Mechanistically, increased primary cilia formation enhanced MAPK and NFkB signaling and increased chromatin accessibility at inflammatory gene loci enriched for AP1 motifs, even in the absence of stimulation, consistent with a chromatin primed state. Higher residual ciliated KC abundance after phototherapy was associated with subsequent treatment escalation. ERK1/2 inhibition reduced cytokine induced primary cilia formation. Conclusions: Ciliated KCs represent an inflammatory epithelial cell state associated with residual disease activity in AD and Pso. The suppression of cytokine-induced primary cilia formation by ERK1/2 inhibition suggests that inflammation associated primary cilia formation may be modifiable process in persistent skin inflammation.

papers.title: Single-cell profiling of endometriosis-associated macrophages and ferroptosis-modulating effects of lemon-derived extracellular vesicles.
papers.authors: Huo L, Zhou Q, Du Y, Chen B, Feng W, He S, Li Y, Chen C, Ning Y.
papers.abstract: Endometriosis is associated with altered immune responses and fibrotic remodeling. We integrated single-cell transcriptomic analysis of eutopic endometrium from women with endometriosis and controls with experimental evaluation of lemon-derived extracellular vesicles (LDEVs). Transcriptomic analysis identified an oxidative stress-associated macrophage state and predicted altered interactions with stromal and epithelial cells. Integrative analysis highlighted ACSL1 as a candidate ferroptosis-related molecular node. In RAW264.7 macrophages, LDEVs increased GPX4 mRNA and decreased TFRC and ACSL1 expression. Under RSL3 challenge, LDEV pretreatment attenuated ACSL4 upregulation. In an experimental model of endometriosis, LDEV treatment reduced ectopic lesion burden and collagen deposition, accompanied by increased GPX4 and decreased ACSL1 and ACSL4 staining. These findings support further investigation of LDEVs as a potential non-hormonal therapeutic strategy for endometriosis.

papers.title: MHC-restricted antigen presentation and clonal T-cell immunity after myocardial infarction: mechanisms, evidence gaps, and therapeutic opportunities.
papers.authors: Liu R, Yang K, Sun C, Guo B, Qi X, Liu Y, Li J, Liu Y.
papers.abstract: Myocardial infarction (MI) alters the cardiac immune microenvironment through tissue injury, antigen release, and recruitment of innate and adaptive immune cells. Major histocompatibility complex (MHC)-restricted antigen presentation can connect these events to T-cell responses that influence repair or persistent inflammation. This narrative review examines antigen acquisition, initial T-cell priming in cardiac-draining lymph nodes, and subsequent recognition of peptide-MHC complexes within injured myocardium. We integrate these processes with T-cell receptor (TCR) repertoire studies and a spatial framework encompassing the infarct core, border zone, and remote myocardium. Direct experimental evidence for cardiac antigen-specific responses is distinguished from human repertoire associations, findings in other diseases, and proposed mechanisms. In particular, TCR clonal expansion alone does not establish cardiac antigen specificity, and cardiomyocyte antigen display should be separated from professional antigen-presenting cell function. We also consider vascular and lymphatic remodeling, macrophage heterogeneity, and the effects of sex and age. Therapeutic approaches are evaluated by intervention, model, measured outcome, and evidence context, with particular attention to the cardiac risks of immune checkpoint blockade. This framework identifies the experiments needed to connect antigen identity and clonotype function to ventricular remodeling and to assess selective immune interventions after MI.

papers.title: Carbonic anhydrase 2 positive tumor-associated endothelial cells contribute to anti-PD-1 therapy resistance through TREM2⁺ macrophages in hepatocellular carcinoma.
papers.authors: Zheng Y, Zhou Y, Luo J, Cui P, Huang C, Yu K, Zhang Y, Wen Z, Han J, Jin X, Shi F, Yu M, Wu J, Zhang J, Lu L.
papers.abstract: Introduction Combining PD-1/PD-L1 blockade with anti-angiogenic therapy has transformed treatment for advanced HCC, yet durable responses remain limited. Tumor-associated endothelial cells (TECs) shape the tumor microenvironment, and contribute to immune exclusion and immunotherapy resistance. Nevertheless, TEC subsets and molecular features of immunotherapy failure in HCC are poorly defined. Objectives This study aims to identify specific TEC subsets and elucidate their functional roles underlying immunotherapy failure in HCC. Methods We performed integrative analysis of single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from anti-PD-1-treated HCC to characterize intratumoral cellular heterogeneity and identify TEC subsets associated with treatment response. Cell-cell communication networks were inferred using CellChat. Functional studies were conducted in HUVECs and HLSECs to assess migration, tube formation, and hypoxia responses. Results Single-cell profiling revealed an expansion of TECs and immunosuppressive myeloid populations in nonresponders to anti-PD-1 therapy. Reclustering of endothelial cells identified a carbonic anhydrase 2 positive (CA2⁺) TEC subset enriched in nonresponders and distinguished by a hypoxia-adapted, proangiogenic, and immune-cold transcriptional program. A CA2⁺ TEC signature derived from the top subtype-specific markers predicted poor progression-free survival and nonresponse in the IMbrave150 and GO30140 cohorts. In HUVECs and HLSECs, CA2 promoted endothelial migration and tube formation and was transcriptionally induced by hypoxia via HIF-1α. Cell‒cell communication analysis showed that CA2⁺ TECs exhibited enhanced outgoing signaling toward TREM2⁺ macrophages, with the APP-CD74 axis emerging as a dominant pathway. TREM2⁺ macrophages upregulate CCL18 expression, thereby potentially limiting both the infiltration and cytotoxic function of CD8⁺ T cells. In vivo, pharmacologic CA2 blockade reprogrammed the TME, reduced immunosuppressive myeloid infiltration, and synergized with anti-PD-1 therapy to suppress tumor growth. Conclusions Our study identifies CA2⁺ TECs as a distinct subset contributing to immunotherapy resistance in HCC through pro-angiogenic and immunosuppressive mechanisms. Targeting CA2 presents a promising approach to enhance the efficacy of PD-1 blockade in patients with HCC.

papers.title: A single-cell lung cancer atlas reveals cellular and molecular drivers of metastasis and clinical outcome.
papers.authors: Jurmeister P, Keyl P, Mochmann LH, Bergmayr L, Schleich K, Chimal Calderon E, Engelhardt-Schott F, Klingler D, Papić D, Wolff J, Fritz R, Keyl J, Merkelbach-Bruse S, Quaas A, Schlachtenberger G, Heldwein M, Rückert JC, Dernbach G, Reinmuth N, Grohé C, Büttner R, Horst D, Frost N, Harter PN, Müller KR, Schallenberg S, Klauschen F.
papers.abstract: Non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, characterized by extensive cellular and molecular heterogeneity. Here, to capture this complexity, we present LuCaS+, a multicenter single-cell RNA sequencing atlas comprising over 2.5 million nuclei from 454 clinically annotated patients with NSCLC with long-term follow-up. LuCaS+ consists of a discovery dataset (Berlin and Cologne, 364 patients) and an independent validation dataset (Munich, 90 patients). Leveraging this dataset, we identified tumor subpopulations with high metastatic potential associated with oncogenic signaling, immune evasion and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. In early-stage adenocarcinoma (lung adenocarcinoma), these cells showed strong prognostic value. Integrating tumor and microenvironmental cell profiles improved survival prediction across all stages, identifying distinct tumor-immune-stromal interaction patterns. These included monocyte- and fibroblast-driven inflammation (lung adenocarcinoma), VEGF-TGFβ-mediated angiogenic feedback loops (lung squamous cell carcinoma) and immune-permissive niches promoting antitumor immunity. LuCaS+ offers a clinically anchored single-cell resource to enable personalized, biology-driven therapies in NSCLC.

papers.title: Transcriptional regulation of NK cell state by ELF4 links innate immune licensing to kidney fibrosis.
papers.authors: Li S, Hu H, Lanzar ZR, Gu X, Cruz-Morales E, Bochi-Layec AC, Sanchez-Navarro A, Park J, Shrestha R, Liu H, Donner AJ, Lin MH, Bell TA, Miner JH, Ruella M, Vivier E, Lucas CL, Hunter CA, Susztak K.
papers.abstract: Fibrosis is a common outcome of chronic tissue injury, yet immune regulators that are conserved across species and translatable to human disease remain poorly defined. By integrating human kidney transcriptomes with multiple murine models of kidney fibrosis, we identified the ETS transcription factor ELF4 as a conserved, immune-enriched regulator associated with disease severity. ELF4 expression was highest in natural killer (NK) cells. Genetic deletion of Elf4, including NK cell-specific ablation, attenuated experimental kidney injury, with reduced inflammation, fibrosis, and loss of renal function. Single-cell and functional analyses showed that ELF4 deficiency disrupts late-stage NK cell maturation and broadly suppresses cytotoxic and interferon-γ (IFNγ) effector programs. Mechanistically, ELF4 directly sustains STAT1 transcription, maintaining a STAT1-TBX21 program required for NK cell maturation and effector competence. Consistent with this framework, NK cell depletion, IFNγ neutralization, or antisense-mediated suppression of Elf4 phenocopied renal protection. Together, these findings identify ELF4 as a transcriptional licensing factor that links NK cell state to kidney injury and highlight innate immune programming as a potential therapeutic entry point in chronic kidney disease.

papers.title: Spatial Niches Shape Function in the Intratumoral Microbiome: From Multiscale Mapping to Niche-Informed Therapy.
papers.authors: Dong L, Song Y, Li X, Wu J, Luo X, Du Y, Xu T.
papers.abstract: Most studies of the intratumoral microbiome describe microbial composition and abundance but do not reveal where bacteria are located within the tumor microenvironment. Evidence that microbial signals vary across tumor regions and host-cell compartments makes spatial context essential to biological interpretation. In this review, we organize evidence at three levels: tissue niches reflect oxygenation, perfusion, pH, necrosis, and anatomy, cellular niches involve malignant, immune, and stromal cells, and physical interfaces include intracellular residence, extracellular association, biofilms, and diffusible products. We examine how contamination-aware sequencing, single-cell host-microbe profiling, spatial transcriptomics, and imaging distinguish detection from localization and relate microbial geography to host-cell states. Spatial organization may affect oncogenic signaling, cytoskeletal remodeling, DNA damage, immune regulation, metastatic fitness, and treatment response. The same bacterial strain may exert opposing immune effects inside and outside host cells. This framework clarifies therapeutic implications. Engineered bacteria can deliver payloads to hypoxic, poorly perfused regions, whereas intracellular nanocarriers, species-selective phages, and biofilm-disrupting platforms address different microbial reservoirs. Major limitations include low-biomass contamination, uncertain viability, incomplete localization, limited causal evidence, and poorly resolved temporal dynamics. Integrating microbial identity with location and physical state should yield more mechanistic models of the intratumoral microbiome and better-defined therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: Identifying crosstalk genes between bipolar disorder and osteoporosis via machine learning and experimental validation.
papers.authors: Wan W, Zhang H, Qiu S, Gu Y.
papers.abstract: Bipolar disorder (BD) has been recognized as an independent risk factor for osteoporosis (OP), yet the shared genetic and molecular mechanisms underlying their comorbidity remain largely unexplored. This study aimed to identify potential crosstalk genes between BD and OP using bioinformatics and machine learning, and to validate their expression patterns in an established in vitro osteoporotic cell model. Gene expression profiles of BD and OP were retrieved from the GEO database; differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were screened and subjected to functional enrichment analysis, and three machine-learning approaches-LASSO, SVM-RFE, and Random Forest-were integrated to identify core crosstalk genes. An H₂O₂-induced osteoporotic model was constructed in MC3T3 E1(14) osteoblasts, and the protein expression of PLXNA2, ROR1, and TAS2R14 was measured by Western blot; protein-protein interaction (PPI) network and immune cell infiltration analyses were also conducted. A total of 20 shared DEGs were identified, from which PLXNA2, ROR1, and TAS2R14 were screened as candidate crosstalk genes. In the cellular model, PLXNA2 and TAS2R14 were significantly downregulated, whereas ROR1 was markedly upregulated, consistent with expression trends observed in clinical OP specimens, and these genes were functionally associated with neural development, metabolic regulation, and immune infiltration. In conclusion, PLXNA2, ROR1, and TAS2R14 may represent candidate crosstalk genes implicated in the comorbidity of BD and OP, and their expression patterns were preliminarily supported in an in vitro osteoporotic cell model. These findings provide potential molecular clues for BD-related OP, although further functional and clinical validation is required.

papers.title: Comprehensive Analysis Identifies FCER1A as a Potential Link Between Immune Dysregulation and Therapeutic Responses in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and Gastric Cancer.
papers.authors: Liang T, Cui Y, Song H.
papers.abstract: Introduction Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients exhibit an elevated risk of gastric cancer (GC), yet the molecular mechanisms underlying this comorbidity remain poorly understood. This study presents a novel integrative bioinformatics framework to identify shared molecular signatures between SLE and GC and to assess their prognostic implications. Methods This study retrieved microarray data from the GSE50772 and GSE81622 datasets in the GEO database and RNA-seq data from the GC cohort in TCGA. Following screening, this study identified differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and further characterized them based on their differential expression. This study identified the common DEGs (co-DEGs) and performed GO and KEGG pathway analyses to identify relevant pathways, immune infiltration, and gene diagnostic value in the context of SLE and GC. Results By analyzing three independent datasets (GSE50772, GSE81622, and TCGA_STAD), this study identified 12 co-DEGs, among which FCER1A was validated as an independent prognostic factor for GC through multivariate Cox regression (HR = 1.184, P = 0.026). In addition, FCER1A expression showed significant positive correlations with infiltration of multiple immune cell types, including macrophages (P = 3.38e-27, r = 0.52, 95% CI: 0.44-0.59), CD4+ T cells (P = 7.32e-18, r = 0.43, 95% CI: 0.34-0.51), and neutrophils (P = 5.82e-12, r = 0.35, 95% CI: 0.25-0.43), suggesting its role in shaping the tumor immune microenvironment. Kaplan-Meier analysis confirmed that high FCER1A expression predicted poorer overall survival (P = 0.036) and first progression (P = 0.029). Discussion In this study, FCER1A was identified as the key gene affected by the combination of SLE and GC. Conclusion This study is the first to systematically link FCER1A-mediated immune infiltration to prognosis in SLE-associated GC, offering a potential biomarker and therapeutic target for this understudied comorbidity.

papers.title: Enhanced Recovery After Surgery in Gastrointestinal Cancer: A Narrative Review of Perioperative Evidence, Compliance-Associated Outcomes, and Geriatric Considerations.
papers.authors: Gao Y, Mu Y, Ren B, Zhou W.
papers.abstract: Purpose of review Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) has become an important component of perioperative care in gastrointestinal oncology, although its implementation remains challenging because of heterogeneous patient profiles. This review critically examines current perioperative evidence, integrates the 2025 ERAS Society guidelines, and discusses three key areas for future development in ERAS: frailty-stratified care, compliance-associated clinical outcomes, and the potential effects of ERAS on perioperative inflammation and oncologic recovery. Recent findings Recent evidence highlights three key areas. First, frailty is an important determinant of perioperative vulnerability in older patients, and Geriatric 8 (G8) screening combined with geriatric co-management can help identify vulnerable individuals and guide individualized perioperative care. Second, ERAS compliance shows a graded association with postoperative morbidity, while machine learning-based analyses suggest that patient characteristics are associated with differences in adherence and recovery trajectories, supporting the implementation of risk-stratified pathways. Third, clinical studies have reported reductions in postoperative inflammatory markers following ERAS implementation, providing a biological rationale for further investigating its effects on perioperative immune function. ERAS implementation is also associated with earlier return to intended oncologic therapy (RIOT), although its impact on long-term oncologic outcomes requires further evaluation. The future development of ERAS lies in dynamic, risk-adapted decision-making rather than rigid protocol enforcement. Integrating continuous quality audits, frailty assessment, geriatric co-management, and individualized perioperative interventions provides an important framework for optimizing recovery across diverse patient populations. Further research should clarify the immunological effects of ERAS, determine whether improvements in short-term recovery translate into long-term oncologic benefits, and extend coordinated perioperative care beyond hospital discharge, as explored in the ERAS 3.0 paradigm.

papers.title: Translational science in modern gynecologic oncology trials.
papers.authors: Arend RC, Dave D, Cosgrove CM, Kohn E, Simpkins F, Adams SF, Nasioudis D, Sood AK.
papers.abstract: Translational science is integral in deciding who would benefit the most from novel therapeutics in gynecologic oncology, yet the specimens, assays, and the data behind them are often handled inconsistently as the translational endpoints are planned late. Clinical trials involving PARP-inhibitors, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), and antibody-drug conjugates in ovarian, endometrial, and cervical cancer show that a biomarker can serve as an eligibility criterion, a stratification factor, a pharmacodynamic measure, or an exploratory tool. This review presents an operational framework for integrating translational science into the trial designs from the outset. We define exploratory, integrated, and integral biomarker tiers and tie each to analytical validation, clinical validation, and level of evidence. It proposes minimum standards for tissue and blood biospecimen collection, adequacy, sampling schedule depending on specimen type, pre-analytical variables, clinical annotation, and reporting with BRISQ, SPREC, and the BloodPAC technical data elements. We also cover newer techniques like ctDNA, addressing their intended use, tumor-informed versus tumor-naive assays, and sampling for minimal residual disease. We then review genomic, transcriptomic, spatial, single-cell, proteomic, metabolomic, and functional platforms, and why discovery should not be treated as validation for modern gynecologic oncology trials. Additionally, maintaining standards for data integration, reproducibility, NIH data sharing in NCI-sponsored, industry-sponsored, and institutional trials is crucial. Ultimately, adaptive master protocols and ctDNA-guided trial designs are discussed as future directions as translational endpoints deserve the same prospective planning as the primary clinical endpoint.

papers.title: Integrated Pan-Cancer Analysis and Functional Characterization Identify SHC2 as a Potential Prognostic Biomarker in Colon Adenocarcinoma.
papers.authors: Zhang H, Tian R, Peng J.
papers.abstract: Introduction Colon adenocarcinoma (COAD) remains a major cause of cancer morbidity and mortality. SHC-transforming protein 2 (SHC2) is an adaptor protein whose cancer-type-specific expression and biological relevance, particularly in COAD, are insufficiently defined. Methods This study integrated TCGA-based expression, clinicopathological, and survival analyses with cBioPortal/ GSCA genomic and methylation analyses, xCell and TIMER immune infiltration estimates, GDSC and CTRP pharmacogenomic data, and a Sparkle spatial transcriptomic section. SHC2-associated transcriptional programs were examined in TCGA-COAD, and loss-of-function experiments were performed in HCT116 and RKO cells. Results SHC2 showed heterogeneous expression across cancers. COAD was prioritized because tumor-associated upregulation coincided with stage-related differences and consistently unfavorable survival associations. Genomic, methylation, immune, and drug-response analyses provided context-dependent correlates rather than a uniform pan-cancer pattern. In a COAD spatial section, SHC2 expression colocalized with malignant regions. SHC2-high COAD tumors were enriched for Wnt/β-catenin, TGF-β, and angiogenesis signatures, whereas SHC2 knockdown reduced proliferation, colony formation, migration, and invasion in both cell models. Discussion Convergent computational and in vitro evidence supports SHC2 as a potential prognostic biomarker and candidate regulator of malignant phenotypes in COAD. Causal mechanisms, clinical performance, and therapeutic relevance require validation in independent cohorts, rescue or overexpression systems, and in vivo models. Conclusion The findings define a COAD-centered, hypothesis-generating framework in which SHC2 expression is linked to adverse clinical features and tumor-promoting cellular behavior, while avoiding causal interpretation of the correlative pan-cancer analyses.

papers.title: Molecular Biomarkers and Biosensing Innovations for the Early Diagnosis of Ankylosing Spondylitis: From Molecular Mechanisms to Precision Diagnostics.
papers.authors: Nautiyal D, Chauhan N, Jain U.
papers.abstract: Ankylosing spondylitis is a chronic immune-mediated, inflammatory spondyloarthropathy in which delayed diagnosis remains a major clinical challenge, particularly during the early stages when definitive structural radiographic changes may be absent. Although HLA-B27 represents the most potent genetic association with ankylosing spondylitis, its incomplete penetrance and variability limit its use as a single diagnostic biomarker. This review critically examines the molecular mechanisms underlying HLA-B27-associated disease, evaluates circulating and molecular biomarkers according to their demonstrated clinical roles and assesses the current development of biosensing technologies for their detection. Biomarkers including IL-17, IL-13, TNF-α, MMP-3, calprotectin, microRNAs, and anti-CD74 antibodies reflect complementary aspects of inflammation, immune dysregulation and tissue remodelling; however, their biological association with the disease should not be compared with validated early diagnostic performance. Emerging optical and electrochemical biosensing platforms demonstrate promising analytical sensitivity and potential for rapid and minimally invasive detection. However, much of the available biosensor research remains at the level of analytical feasibility or biomarker detection, with limited evidence demonstrating discrimination of ankylosing spondylitis from clinical controls and very limited independent clinical validation. Major translational barriers include biomarker heterogeneity, sensor standardisation, and clinical testing. Future development should focus on clinically validated multi-biomarker biosensor systems, nanomaterial-enhanced detection and machine learning-assisted analysis. Collectively, the combination of molecular biomarker research and next-generation biosensing technology can elevate diagnostic accuracy, providing early intervention and precision medicine strategies for disease assessment.

papers.title: Mitofusin-2 deficiency impairs neutrophil maturation and reduces non-glucose substrate utilization.
papers.authors: Liu W, Hu L, Chen Y, Zhao M, Fan Z.
papers.abstract: Neutrophils are essential for innate immunity, and they must mature properly to maintain immune homeostasis. Although mitochondrial dynamics influence hematopoietic fate, how specific fusion machinery controls neutrophil development in vivo remains poorly understood. Although our earlier study suggested a role for mitofusin-2 (MFN2) in neutrophil development using cell line models, the need for MFN2 during primary hematopoietic neutrophil maturation and the associated metabolic changes have remained unclear. Using a hematopoietic-specific knockout model (MFN2 flox/flox Vav-iCre +/- ), we found that MFN2 deletion results in the accumulation of immature neutrophils in both the bone marrow and peripheral blood. Surprisingly, MFN2 deficiency was associated with increased mitochondrial membrane potential in immature neutrophils. Super-resolution imaging showed altered mitochondrial morphology characterized by reduced elongation. Functional metabolic profiling using single-cell energetic metabolism by profiling translation inhibition (SCENITH) showed that, despite preserved overall translational activity and mitochondrial contribution, MFN2-deficient neutrophils exhibited selectively reduced utilization of non-glucose substrates, reflected by decreased fatty acid and amino acid oxidation (FAO and AAO)-supported translation in immature and mature neutrophils. Together, these findings identify an association between MFN2 deficiency, impaired neutrophil maturation, and reduced utilization of non-glucose substrates, supporting a potential link between mitochondrial substrate use and terminal neutrophil development.

papers.title: Identification of Candidate Targets and Immune Characteristics of Salvianolic Acid E Against Ulcerative Colitis via Integrative Transcriptomic Analysis and Machine Learning.
papers.authors: Liu Y, Guo B, Yu L, Tang Y, Han C, Zhou Z, Zhang S, He Y.
papers.abstract: Introduction Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease with a complex pathogenesis. This study aims to systematically investigate the mechanism of Salvianolic acid E (SAE) in treating UC by identifying its core molecular targets. Methods Potential target genes of SAE against UC were screened via differential expression analysis of datasets. Integrated approaches including machine learning algorithms, network pharmacology, molecular docking, immune infiltration analysis, and experimental validation were employed to investigate the binding interactions between SAE and target proteins. Results A total of 13 potential target genes were identified. Machine learning further refined these to five core genes (SLC23A1, SLC6A14, LCN2, PLA2G2A, and CASP1) as key regulatory factors. Among them, SLC23A1 was significantly downregulated, whereas the other four were significantly upregulated. Molecular docking showed putative interactions between SAE and the target proteins. Immune infiltration analysis revealed strong correlations between the core genes and immune cells such as M2 macrophages, neutrophils, and resting mast cells. Cellular-level validation confirmed the expression patterns of these key genes. Discussion These five core genes constitute a coordinated pathological axis underlying UC progression, which sequentially involves impaired epithelial barrier function, activated innate immune response, amplified pro-inflammatory lipid signaling, and caspase-1-mediated pyroptosis. The stable binding of SAE to these target proteins supports a multi-target synergistic mechanism: SAE may concurrently correct dysregulated solute transport, suppress pro-inflammatory enzymatic activities, and modulate the colonic immune microenvironment. In particular, the strong associations of core genes with neutrophils, M2 macrophages, and resting mast cells suggest that immunomodulation may serve as a critical potential dimension of SAE's therapeutic efficacy against UC. Our integrated analytical strategy also provides a replicable paradigm for deciphering the pharmacological mechanisms of multi-target natural compounds. Conclusion The five candidate regulatory genes and the putative binding of SAE to its key targets provide critical insights into the therapeutic mechanism of SAE in UC, offering novel directions for future UC treatment development.

papers.title: S100A11 promotes immunosuppressive tumour-associated macrophage polarisation with SIRT6-associated changes in SMAD3 acetylation and SMAD2/3 activation in colorectal cancer.
papers.authors: Huang Y, Shi X, Hu W, Lin X, Wu Z, Xie H, Xu L, Wang J, Xu L, Zou J.
papers.abstract: Background Colorectal cancer (CRC) develops not only through malignant epithelial cells but also through immune-cell reprogramming within the tumour microenvironment. Tumour-associated macrophages (TAMs) play a central role in mediating immune suppression, but how tumour-associated cues drive their immunosuppressive programming remains poorly defined. Methods Public CRC single-cell transcriptomic analysis, 20 paired CRC and adjacent non-tumour tissues, THP-1-derived macrophage polarisation models, and HCT116-conditioned TAM-like macrophages were analysed. Selected findings were validated in primary human monocyte-derived macrophages and SW480 CRC cells. S100A11 gain- and loss-of-function assays, SIRT6 rescue experiments, coimmunoprecipitation, immunofluorescence, Western blotting, quantitative PCR, flow cytometry, SMAD3 immunoprecipitation, TGF-β neutralisation, and CRC-cell functional assays were performed to investigate the underlying mechanism and functional consequences. An immunodeficient HCT116 xenograft tumour-growth model and an in vitro HCT116/CD8+ T-cell co-culture system were further used to assess tumour growth and CD8+ T-cell activation and effector-marker expression, respectively. Results S100A11 was recurrently detected in monocyte/macrophage compartments across CRC single-cell datasets and was elevated in CRC tissues. High S100A11 expression was associated with CD206+ macrophage-related features. S100A11 enhanced an immunosuppressive macrophage phenotype with increased expression of CD206, PPARG/PPARγ, IL-10, TGF-β, PD-L1 and PD-L2 in macrophage models. Mechanistically, S100A11 associated with SIRT6 and was accompanied by reduced SIRT6-SMAD2/3 association, increased SMAD3 acetylation, and increased SMAD2/3 phosphorylation. SIRT6 overexpression partially reversed S100A11- and TGF-β-induced macrophage polarisation. Conditioned medium from S100A11-overexpressing TAM-like macrophages increased HCT116 proliferation, clonogenicity, migration, and invasion, reduced apoptosis, promoted HCT116 xenograft growth, and suppressed CD8+ T-cell activation and effector-marker expression in vitro. These effects were attenuated by SIRT6 overexpression in TAM-like macrophages. TGF-β neutralisation attenuated the conditioned-medium-induced increase in HCT116 proliferation and partially restored CD8+ T-cell CD69 expression. Conclusions S100A11 is a macrophage-associated regulator of immunosuppressive TAM polarisation in CRC and may contribute to tumour-promoting macrophage reprogramming within the tumour microenvironment. These findings suggest that the S100A11-SIRT6-SMAD3 pathway warrants further investigation as a potential target for macrophage reprogramming in the colorectal cancer immune microenvironment.

papers.title: Jiangtang Pill for Type 2 Diabetes: Network Pharmacology and Transcriptomics.
papers.authors: Liu R, Zhang M, Zhao Y, Dong H, Si H, Niu Y.
papers.abstract: Introduction This study computationally explores the polypharmacological mechanisms of Jiangtang Pill (JTP) in treating Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) using an integrated in silico approach. Methods Active compounds of JTP and predicted pharmacological targets were extracted from databases. Protein-protein interaction networks identified core hubs, which were intersected with DEGs from a T2DM transcriptomic dataset (GSE15932). Functional mechanisms were evaluated via GO and KEGG analyses. Immune infiltration was assessed using CIBERSORT. Molecular docking and 100-ns Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations were performed to evaluate the predicted binding interactions and dynamic behavior of key ligand-protein complexes. Results AKT1, MAPK3, STAT3, and TNF emerged as candidate targets supported by the integrated network and transcriptomic analyses. Functional enrichment highlighted the PI3K-Akt, AGE-RAGE, and MAPK pathways. CIBERSORT analysis indicated a lower estimated abundance of CD4+ memory activated T cells in T2DM, which was inversely associated with the expression of selected targets. The 100-ns MD simulations showed that the four ligand-protein complexes remained dynamically associated throughout the trajectories, with distinct RMSD, RMSF, compactness, and hydrogen-bonding profiles for β-sitosterol and kaempferol. Discussion By integrating network pharmacology, clinical transcriptomics, and structural analyses, this study supports a hypothesis that JTP may influence metabolic and immune-related pathways involved in T2DM. Conclusion These findings provide a testable computational framework for the potential multi-target actions of JTP and warrant further experimental validation.

papers.title: Placental Glycolysis-Related Transcriptional Features in Early-Onset Preeclampsia Complicated by Fetal Growth Restriction.
papers.authors: Zhang R, Peng Y, Gao Y, Kong W, Lin B, Deng M, Chen Z, Liu Y, Liu Q.
papers.abstract: Background Preeclampsia (PE) is a severe obstetric complication characterized by the new onset of hypertension and proteinuria after 20 weeks of gestation. However, bulk transcriptomic approaches cannot resolve cell type-specific alterations within the heterogeneous placenta. Single- cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables gene expression profiling at individual-cell resolution, thereby revealing cellular heterogeneity and identifying cell populations and pathways potentially involved in disease processes. Methods This exploratory study integrated scRNA-seq data from one EOPE-FGR placental sample and one healthy control sample with bulk RNA-seq data. The Seurat and limma packages were used for single-cell and bulk transcriptomic analyses, respectively. Gene set enrichment analysis and differential expression analysis were performed to identify candidate pathways and genes. RT-qPCR was used to examine candidate gene expression, whereas the Cell Counting Kit-8 assay was used to assess the effect of FLT1 knockdown on cell viability under hypoxia/reoxygenation conditions. Results Exploratory scRNA-seq analysis identified ten major placental cell types. In the two analyzed samples, the EOPE-FGR sample showed a higher observed EVT proportion, whereas EVT cells displayed sample-specific glycolysis-, interferon-, and immune-related expression patterns. These single-cell observations were treated as exploratory. An exploratory intersection of bulk disease- versus-control differentially expressed genes with genes identified from the EVT high- versus low-glycolysis-score comparison prioritized 11 candidate genes: FLT1, PROCR, INHA, CST6, HTRA1, C12orf75, FSTL3, INHBA, CDA, EBI3, and PRG2. In supportive in vitro experiments, eight selected genes showed increased expression under hypoxia/reoxygenation conditions, and FLT1 knockdown was associated with an increased CCK-8 signal. The CCK-8 assay did not directly assess glycolytic activity. Discussion Bulk RNA-seq analysis identified glycolysis-related enrichment in EOPE-FGR placentas, whereas the single-cell datasets provided exploratory observations of EVT-associated expression patterns. Given the limited scRNA-seq sample size, these observations should be regarded as hypothesis-generating and require validation in larger independent cohorts. Conclusion The integrated analyses prioritized candidate genes associated with bulk disease-related and within-sample EVT glycolysis-score-related expression patterns. These exploratory findings do not establish a causal relationship between FLT1, glycolytic activity, and immune alterations and require validation in larger cohorts and through direct metabolic assays.

papers.title: Cell-Cell Communication Network Analysis of Tertiary Lymphoid Structures in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer.
papers.authors: Meng M, Li Y.
papers.abstract: Introduction Tertiary Lymphoid Structures (TLS) are associated with a favorable prognosis in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC). However, the mechanisms governing their formation, particularly the existence of breast cancer subtype-specific critical cell communication networks, remain unclear. This study aims to systematically decipher the specific cellular interaction networks associated with TLS in TNBC and Estrogen Receptor-positive Breast Cancer (ER+ BC). Materials and methods Public spatial transcriptomics (TNBC: GSE210616; ER+ BC: 10x Genomics public Visium dataset) and single-cell transcriptomics (GSE176078) data were integrated to attribute TLS-associated genes to their cell-type origins and infer intercellular communication. TLS regions were independently identified by two pathologists based on H&E images (TNBC: 7 TLS; ER+ BC: 12 TLS), followed by differential expression analysis. Using single-cell data, a dual-criterion (expression rate ≥20% and average expression level ≥ upper quartile) was employed for cell-type expression attribution, with sensitivity analysis across thresholds. Cell-cell communication network inference and quantitative analysis were performed based on an expanded ligand-receptor database (CellTalkDB, 3,398 pairs), and the core findings were cross-validated using CellChat. Results TLS in TNBC exhibited a far more active transcriptional state compared to ER+ Breast Cancer (ER+ BC), with 198 vs 29 differentially expressed genes. Interaction network analysis revealed that in TNBC TLS, fibroblasts (cancer-associated fibroblasts, CAFs) constituted the dominant core signaling hub (net signal output strength: +458.7), whereas endothelial cells were the predominant net signal receiver (net output: -808.6). In contrast, TLS in ER+ BC were characterized by interactions predominantly involving fibroblasts (dominant output, +261.1) and plasma cells (dominant reception, -127.0). Cell-type expression attribution further confirmed that TLS-associated signals in TNBC predominantly originated from fibroblasts (70.3% of core TLS genes). Discussion Our intercellular communication analysis reveals a stark subtype-specific landscape: TLSs in TNBC are predominantly characterized by a fibroblast (CAF)-centered signaling hub, whereas TLS in ER+ BC features a fibroblast-plasma cell axis. The association between the TLS-related transcriptional signature and immune cytolytic activity was further supported in the independent The Cancer Genome Atlas breast cancer cohort (r = 0.747, P Conclusion This study identifies a TNBC-specific fibroblast (CAF)-centered communication hub as a prominent feature of TLS-associated intercellular networks, offering prioritized candidate axes warranting further functional validation for potential immunotherapy development.

papers.title: Multi-omics profiling suggests deep brain stimulation-associated expansion of CLIC3+ NK cells attenuates neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease.
papers.authors: Zhang S, Luo Z, Tan Y, Cheng B, Xiao W, Jiang G, Zhu T.
papers.abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) alleviates Parkinson's disease (PD) symptoms, but its immunomodulatory mechanisms remain elusive. Through integrating microarray (GSE23676), single cell/nucleus RNA-seq (GSE184950, GSE202210, GSE223138, GSE243639; after quality control (mitochondrial gene content 200) 616,076 high-quality cells were included), and GWAS data, we identified CLIC3 as a DBS-associated, potential protective implications in PD. CLIC3 was selectively up-regulated in a distinct natural killer cell subset (NK_CLIC3), which secreted TGFB1 to restrain neuroinflammation. CellChat and immunohistochemistry revealed that NK_CLIC3 cells communicated with PD-relevant neuronal populations: excitatory (SLC18A2+), inhibitory (SLC18A2+), oligodendrocyte (SLC18A2+), and astrocytic (SLC18A2+) cells via THY1-ADGRE5 and GZMA-PARD3 axes. Immune infiltration analysis (GSE114517; n = 75) suggested NK infiltration and deficient M2 macrophage recruitment in PD brains, underscoring an inadequate anti-inflammatory response. We further isolated CLIC3-positive NK cells (from a healthy donor) by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) and confirmed their ability to degrade α-synuclein, the pathological protein in Parkinson's disease, supporting the potential NK(CLIC3+) cells' protective function in PD. Our findings suggest DBS may expand NK_CLIC3 cells to suppress neuroinflammation through TGFB1 mediated immune-neuronal crosstalk, positioning CLIC3 as a prospective therapeutic target for PD.

papers.title: Integrating computational and experimental approaches to identify antigen-specific antibodies.
papers.authors: Abbate MF, Pereira P, Toxe P, Maestrali N, Gagnaire M, Vigne E, Shahsavarian MA, Mora T, Walczak AM.
papers.abstract: The identification of therapeutic antibodies is critical for developing effective treatments for many diseases. We present a joint computational and experimental approach for identifying antigen-specific antibodies. We develop and test our pipeline on a probe antigen: GFRAL fused with Diphtheria Toxin Fragment A (DTA). Using humanized Trianni mice, we conducted a longitudinal study with repeated blood sampling and splenic analysis. We applied the STAR computational method that exploits similarity network properties on bulk antibody repertoire data sampled at key time points. By mapping the output from STAR to single cell data taken at the last time point, we successfully identified a pool of antibodies, of which 45% demonstrated binding capabilities. We observed convergent selection, where responding sequences with identical amino acid complementarity determining regions 3 (CDR3) were found in different mice. We provide a catalog of 70 experimentally validated antibodies against the GFRAL-DTA fusion antigen. This study underscores the utility of integrating computational methods and experimental validation for antibody discovery in therapeutic contexts by reducing time and increasing efficiency.

papers.title: An interpretable machine learning model for predicting response to anti-GD2 combined with umbilical cord blood-derived natural killer cell immunotherapy in neuroblastoma.
papers.authors: Dong Q, Song M, Mai Y, Wang J, Zhu J, Lu S, Sun F, Huang J, Zhen Z, Tan X, Zhang Y, Que Y, Lan Y, Cao Y, Deng F, Qin H, Zhang Y, Xiang T.
papers.abstract: Background Neuroblastoma remains a major therapeutic challenge for children with high-risk or relapsed/refractory disease. Anti-GD2 therapy combined with umbilical cord blood-derived natural killer (UCB-NK) cell therapy represents an emerging strategy, but responses vary substantially. Imaging and bone marrow assessments require specialized resources, creating a need for complementary tools based on routinely available data. However, whether serial routine peripheral blood measurements can support response prediction in this treatment setting remains unclear. Methods Serial peripheral blood measurements from 42 patients were used to derive dynamic coupling features that reflected longitudinal trends and coordinated changes between biomarkers. These features were integrated with static variables to develop machine learning models for response prediction. Seven machine learning models were compared using the same repeated stratified cross-validation framework. Model selection considered discrimination, probability-estimation quality, and interpretability. SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) was used to interpret the final model. Results Considering cross-validated performance, the quality of probability estimates, and clinical interpretability, L2-regularized logistic regression was selected as the final model for response prediction. The model leveraged dynamic peripheral blood features to predict response to anti-GD2 combined with UCB-NK cell immunotherapy, achieving a cross-validated AUC of 0.873 (95% bootstrap CI, 0.735-0.976) and a Brier score of 0.131 (95% bootstrap CI, 0.087-0.182). SHAP analysis characterized the direction and magnitude of feature contributions to model predictions. Conclusion This study developed an interpretable response-prediction model using serial routine peripheral blood tests obtained in clinical practice. The model may complement treatment-response assessment using routinely available data. However, validation in larger, independent cohorts is required before clinical use.

papers.title: Single-cell transcriptomic analysis of the immune response to CHIKV infection.
papers.authors: Huang P, Wang H, Xu S, Li M, Guo M, Wang H, Gou X, Wang C, He Y, Pan W.
papers.abstract: Background The Chikungunya virus (CHIKV), a re-emerging mosquito-borne alphavirus, is responsible for acute febrile illness and severe polyarthralgia. Although both innate and adaptive immune responses influence the disease outcomes, the detailed cellular immunopathogenesis of CHIKV in peripheral blood is not yet fully elucidated. Methods We profiled PBMCs from 29 patients with acute CHIKV infection and 10 controls via single-cell RNA sequencing. Between-group analyses treated donors as biological replicates, incorporating pseudobulk differential expression analysis as well as donor-level comparisons of pathway scores and cell proportions. Orthogonal validation was performed using qPCR and ELISA, and an exploratory analysis was conducted on a publicly available DENV dataset. Results Interferon-response signatures were upregulated across the majority of PBMC populations, with particularly prominent signals observed in monocytes and NK cells. Differences in relative cell composition were detected in descriptive statistics, but did not retain statistical significance after donor-level multiple testing correction. B-cell immunoglobulin isotypes varied across cell subsets, and their transcripts did not allow determination of antigen specificity. Cross-study analysis of DENV did not support the quantitative conclusion that the CHIKV-induced immune response is stronger. Conclusions Acute CHIKV infection is associated with a broad interferon-stimulated transcriptional program in PBMCs. Conclusions drawn from cross-sectional and cross-study comparisons require cautious interpretation.

papers.title: Mutational binding assessment for TCR engineering on experimental and AlphaFold 3 scaffolds.
papers.authors: Guo Z, Oyama K, Yamaguchi R.
papers.abstract: Machine learning-based binding affinity prediction can support T-cell receptor (TCR) engineering, but its reliability remains uncertain when experimental structures of TCRs bound to peptide-major histocompatibility complexes (pMHCs) are unavailable and predicted structures must be used instead. Here, we examined how AlphaFold 3 (AF3) scaffold choice and conformational sampling affect ΔΔG -based prioritization of TCR-pMHC complementarity-determining region (CDR) mutations. Bound-unbound structural comparisons showed that pMHC binding is associated mainly with local CDR remodeling, especially in CDR3 loops, whereas TCR framework regions remain comparatively stable. AF3 generally recovered bound-like TCR conformations, but downstream ΔΔG prediction performance depended strongly on both scaffold source and model architecture. These scaffold-dependent differences indicate that experimental structures remain the most reliable input when available, although such structures are rarely accessible in prospective TCR design settings. Among AF3-based inputs, Prompt-DDG and RDE-PPI were relatively robust to wild-type predicted scaffolds, whereas BA-DDG and H3-DDG benefited more from mutant-specific AF3 scaffolds evaluated by reverse-mutation scoring. Across four templates, AF3-mutant scaffolds gave the highest mean top-10 recovery among the AF3-based inputs for all four predictors. These results support using experimental structures when available and suggest using AF3-mutant scaffolds for recovering top-ranked CDR candidates when only predicted structures are available.

papers.title: Liver immune tolerance and regulated cell death in transplantation and hepatocellular carcinoma: shared mechanisms, divergent outcomes.
papers.authors: Wang Y, Zhang H, Dong F, Xu H, Huang F, Jia B.
papers.abstract: The liver constantly encounters gut-derived antigens, microbial molecules, and food antigens. This environment has shaped a tissue-specific tolerance network centered on tolerogenic antigen presentation, immune-checkpoint activation, regulatory cell expansion, and metabolic suppression. This feature protects the liver during prolonged inflammation and gives it an immunological identity that most solid organs lack. Regulated cell death (RCD) and dead-cell clearance form a critical mechanistic layer within this network. Efficient efferocytosis of apoptotic cells reinforces resolution and tolerance, whereas necroptosis, pyroptosis, and ferroptosis disrupt cell membranes and release danger signals that reshape myeloid activation, T-cell function, and the tumor microenvironment. In liver transplantation, this tolerogenic tendency produces donor-specific hyporesponsiveness, allowing a selected subset of stable recipients to stop immunosuppression while maintaining graft function-a state called operational tolerance. In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), tumors exploit the same immunosuppressive axes to block anti-tumor T-cell infiltration and effector function. Anti-PD-L1 therapy combined with anti-angiogenic treatment improves survival, demonstrating that partial disruption of tumor immunosuppression is therapeutically effective. Spatial transcriptomics and single-cell sequencing reveal that SPP1-positive macrophages and cancer-associated fibroblasts form a tumor immune barrier that excludes lymphocytes, showing that hepatic tolerance is organized in space. This duality becomes most dangerous in HCC recurrence after liver transplantation, where immune checkpoint inhibitors boost anti-tumor immunity but also raise the risk of acute rejection, graft failure, and death. Unlike reviews focused on hepatic immune tolerance, regulated cell death, or HCC immunobiology in isolation, this review integrates these processes across the physiological liver, transplantation, HCC, and post-transplant recurrence. We define this coordinated hyporesponsive state as the liver immune tolerance program (ITP), generated by cellular, molecular, spatial, metabolic, and cell-death-related networks. Rather than treating these processes separately, we position RCD and dead-cell clearance as a "death-to-immunity axis," systematically compare ITP remodeling in the physiological liver, transplantation, and HCC, and use post-transplant HCC recurrence as a clinical crossover setting in which graft protection and antitumor immune surveillance become therapeutic considerations. On this basis, we propose precision immune homeostasis: rather than choosing between immunosuppression and immune activation, immune status should be adjusted to an individualized range that protects the graft while preserving anti-tumor immune surveillance.

papers.title: Integrating ferroptosis and the tumor-immune gene mutations interface: a novel lenvatinib resistance prognostic signature with YWHAB-related immunotherapeutic correlates in hepatocellular carcinoma.
papers.authors: Yu H, Wang Z, Zou H, Liu H, Ma Y, Cao B, Wen J, Aili A.
papers.abstract: Background Lenvatinib resistance represents a major clinical challenge in the treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), necessitating the identification of strategies to overcome this issue. Although ferroptosis, a non-apoptotic cell death process, is implicated in the progression of HCC and the response to lenvatinib, the prognostic relevance and the lenvatinib response-related mechanisms of ferroptosis-related genes (FRGs) remain poorly understood. Methods An eight-gene ferroptotic lenvatinib-related prognostic signature (FLRPS) was developed as a prognostic model. Based on the median risk score, the patients were classified into high-risk and low-risk groups to compare clinical outcomes, immune traits, and mutational profiles. Immunohistochemistry, spatial transcriptome analysis and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) were used to identify the specificity of YWHAB expression in HCC. In vitro and in vivo assays were utilized to evaluate the impact of YWHAB on the phenotypes of HCC cells and lenvatinib-induced ferroptosis, as well as to investigate the underlying mechanisms. Results The FLRPS, comprising eight genes (CENPA, RAN, CDCA8, KIF2C, YWHAB, HDAC2, DYNC1H1, and NRAS), yielded scores that positively correlated with poorer prognosis, advanced pathological grade, later clinical stage, metrics of genomic instability, and lower M2 macrophage infiltration. Furthermore, a nomogram integrating the FLRPS and tumor stage accurately predicted overall survival. Additionally, lenvatinib-resistant HCC samples exhibited elevated YWHAB expression. Downregulation of YWHAB sensitized Hepa1-6 cells to lenvatinib both in vitro and in vivo , an effect accompanied by decreased GPX4 levels and reversed by liproxstatin-1, suggesting a ferroptosis-related mechanism involving PI3K/AKT pathway inhibition. Conclusions The FLRPS serves as an effective predictive model for the prognosis of HCC. Targeting YWHAB may represent a promising therapeutic strategy to overcome lenvatinib resistance in HCC.

papers.title: Integrated bioinformatics analysis identifies a ubiquitination-related gene signature in schizophrenia with peripheral clinical validation.
papers.authors: Bi X, Li B, Lv M, Yang J, Qiao D.
papers.abstract: Background Dysregulation of the ubiquitin proteasome pathway is implicated in the pathogenesis of schizophrenia (SCZ). The objective of this study is to identify the dysregulation of the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway and the potential mechanisms associated with SCZ by comprehensive analysis using integrated GEO datasets. Methods We integrated three SCZ related datasets containing 1847 ubiquitination-related genes (URGs) from GeneCards and PubMed, addressing batch effects and normalization with R packages. Subsequent Gene Ontology enrichment analysis was applied to the identified URGs, and an 8-gene molecular signature was constructed to distinguish schizophrenia from control brain tissues, and the discriminatory performance was evaluated by the area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve. SCZ samples were categorized into high-risk and low-risk groups based on median Risk Scores, followed by gene set enrichment analysis. Results A total of 13 SCZ-associated ubiquitin-related differentially expressed genes were significantly identified, with eleven being extremely statistically significant and two highly statistically significant. An 8-gene LASSO-derived molecular signature was constructed and validated, effectively discriminating SCZ patients from controls and classifying SCZ patients into high-risk and low-risk subgroups. The study also constructed protein-protein interaction and regulatory networks and conducted immune infiltration analysis, indicating statistically significant differences in six types of immune cells between the SCZ group and the control group, including CD56bright natural killer cells and central memory CD4+ T cells. ELISA validation in an independent clinical cohort confirmed elevated plasma S100A8 in SCZ patients versus controls, with no significant correlation to PANSS five-factor scores, suggesting S100A8 as a candidate peripheral biomarker reflecting disease state rather than current symptom severity. Conclusions Together with the identification of 13 ubiquitination-related DEGs and an eight-gene LASSO signature demonstrating moderate discriminative accuracy for stratifying SCZ patients, this multi-faceted analysis reveals altered ubiquitination patterns in SCZ and provides a hypothesis-generating foundation for future prospective studies incorporating drug-naïve first-episode patients, longitudinal sampling, and appropriate disease controls.

papers.title: Comprehensive profiling of immune landscape changes and oxidative stress-associated biomarkers in intervertebral disc degeneration.
papers.authors: Huang J, Gong F, Li J, Lu S, Li X, Zhao J, Bai Y, Gu X.
papers.abstract: Background Intervertebral disc degeneration (IDD) is often considered a cause of low back pain. Oxidative stress and the dysregulation of the immune microenvironment are well recognized as important players in this pathology. However, the global knowledge about the core genes that are related to the oxidative stress and how they are involved in the immune response is still missing. Methods We integrated transcriptomic data from three IDD cohorts (GSE167199, GSE176205, GSE186542) and performed differential expression analysis, WGCNA, consensus clustering, and CIBERSORT to identify oxidative stress-related genes, define molecular subtypes, and evaluate immune infiltration. We further constructed single-gene GSEA models, ceRNA networks, and TF-mRNA interactions. Biomarker validity was tested via qPCR and IHC in human samples, and immunofluorescence in a rat puncture model. Results The study revealed two novel IDD subtypes with distinct oxidative stress signatures, and identified CD36, SESN3, and HMOX1 as key regulators. Their expression correlated with immune infiltration, particularly resting mast cells, naïve CD4 + T cells, and macrophages. GSEA linked them to cell cycle, metabolism, and cytokine pathways, while ceRNA and TF networks revealed complex regulation involving lncRNAs, miRNAs, and transcription factors. Validation confirmed their upregulation in human and rat degenerated discs, highlighting their diagnostic and therapeutic potential. Conclusion The study used bioinformatics to identify and suggest CD36, SESN3 and HMOX1 as potential oxidative stress-associated biomarkers in IDD, and also underlines their strong relationship with the remodeling of the immune microenvironment. These results contribute to a better understanding of the relationship between oxidative processes and immune response in the context of the disc degeneration, and may help to conceive future therapeutic approaches with antioxidant and immunomodulatory effects.
